db958e2353fb73d9: No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers.

Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report. Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.

“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”
d13674531f5e0f24: SHANGHAI: Carlos Alcaraz fell to Zizou Bergs in straight sets at the Shanghai Masters on Monday, interrupting the former world number one's in-form return to the professional Tour after being sidelined for months by injury.
The 39th-ranked Belgian beat the second-seeded Spanish star 7-5, 7-6 (7/4) in the third round to land the tournament's biggest upset yet, and will play either Tommy Paul or Valentin Vacherot next.
"It's a little disbelief and not feeling too much," Bergs, 27, said afterwards.
"You're just really in the moment, being focused on the points you have to play," he added.
Alcaraz started with more quality until Bergs broke the Spaniard's serve to go up 3-2 in the first set.
The 23-year-old grabbed back that break in the next game but was uncharacteristically off-target, sending a mess of shots into the net.
He double-faulted to hand Bergs a critical breakpoint in the 11th game and lost the first set when a volley went short.
Alcaraz was visibly frustrated during the second set as he vented to his corner following a series of misfired shots that left him with no points in the fourth and eighth games.
Alcaraz forced a tie-break but could not reach a third set as Bergs closed things out just past the two-hour mark on his first match point.
3ef54f5cc0b953b9: Not satisfied with shoehorning Copilot into every crevice of Office, Microsoft is adding Office to the Copilot app, while also evicting the AI assistant from certain parts of Outlook. The plan is simple: give the Copilot app a prompt, and it will create an Office document (for example, Word) and let a user edit it in the appropriate Office application while keeping the Copilot conversation going. The document can be shared with other users too, who can use the prompt Copilot to tweak it. Albeit an interesting approach, we suspect the system's reliance on OneDrive, rather than that enterprise favorite, SharePoint, might put off some customers. The new feature is also only rolling out to Frontier customers in Chat and Cowork. There's also a question-mark over Microsoft's commitment. The company is quick to drop or deprecate technology when its attention drifts elsewhere. The ability to create a theme in Outlook with Copilot is an example. Less than two years ago, Microsoft announced "Themes by Copilot in Outlook" which, according to the software and cloud biz, marked "the first instance of dynamic AI-generated theming in productivity applications." Themes by Copilot in Outlook, for users with a Copilot license, was a relatively simple piece of technology and could be dynamic, showing imagery inspired by the user's locale (if location permissions were enabled) and updating at regular intervals, for example, based on the current weather. It was all terribly exciting, and Microsoft imagined a world where users might fiddle with their productivity applications in the same way that "you might accent your desk with a candle or photos, spruce up your office with artwork or plants." After all, what's better than watching a beautiful sunset while Outlook quietly explodes in the background? However, after less than two years, the feature is for the chop, according to a post in Microsoft's Message Center. "Themes by Copilot," it wrote at the weekend, "will be removed from Settings, and users will no longer be able to select or return to a Theme by Copilot after changing to a different theme." If you're currently using a Theme by Copilot, it won't go anywhere until you change it, but after that, there's no going back. It's unclear why Microsoft is retiring the feature so soon after announcing it. It might be due to low usage (we can imagine some administrators weren't happy that users could override the selected appearance of their tools) or a step back from the Copilot All The Things approach Microsoft has taken in recent years. It is, however, a salutary warning for anyone enthusiastically embracing Office in Copilot, an interesting feature that will make for some impressive keynotes. It will also need to demonstrate its worth or face the same fate as Themes by Copilot when Microsoft moves on to The Next Big Thing. ®
8992b39eb57adf7f: SINGAPORE, Oct 12 — Prevailing weather and haze conditions have forced Firefly to extend flight cancellations between Subang and Singapore’s Seletar Airport until October 14, with affected passengers being offered alternative Malaysia Airlines flights, subject to seat availability, or full refunds.

Firefly, a wholly owned subsidiary of Malaysia Airlines, had earlier cancelled all scheduled flights between Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport in Subang and Seletar Airport from October 10 to 12 as a precautionary safety measure.

In an advisory on Monday, the airline said the extended cancellations involved six daily services: FY3122 and FY3123, FY3124 and FY3125, FY3126 and FY3127, FY3128 and FY3129, FY3130 and FY3131, as well as FY3132 and FY3133.
“Affected passengers are being contacted and reallocated onto available Malaysia Airlines services via the Kuala Lumpur-Singapore route, subject to seat availability.
“Passengers who opt not to proceed with the reallocated flights are eligible for a full refund, which will be credited back to the original payment method within 30 working days,” it said.

Meanwhile, Singapore’s air quality remained unhealthy on Monday, with the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) ranging from 118 to 155 as of 7 pm, according to the National Environment Agency (NEA).
Readings stood at 155 in the central and west regions, 139 in the east, 122 in the south and 118 in the north. — Bernama

a458452e92f4015e: ALOR SETAR: An 18-year-old youth, whose body was found dumped by the roadside in Gurun, was allegedly held captive and tortured for two days, says Kedah police chief Adzli Abu Shah.
Adzli said the victim was abducted in Pendang on Oct 5 by a group of suspects who accused him of stealing a motorcycle.

“The victim was taken to the house of one of the suspects, where he was detained for two days, tortured and beaten, and had his hair cut,” he told reporters at the Kedah police headquarters here today.
The victim was found dead in the house on the night of Oct 7. Those who tortured him then decided to dump his body by the roadside along Jalan Harvard in Gurun.
Police received information about the discovery of the body at 8.05am on Oct 8.
A post-mortem found that the victim died from blunt force trauma to the head.
Adzli said police arrested 14 people, aged between 16 and 24, in operations around Gurun and Guar Chempedak on Oct 8, a few hours after the body was discovered.
Police seized 14 mobile phones, a car, a pair of scissors, and the victim’s identity card.
Twelve suspects have been remanded for six days until Wednesday, while two minors have been remanded until tomorrow.
The case is being investigated for murder under Section 302 of the Penal Code.
The victim was found wearing yellow and black sportswear and had injuries to his head and face. He was initially found without identification documents.

In a separate case, Adzli said police were tracking down two men to assist in investigations into an attempted murder and the obstruction of police officers during an operation against migrant smuggling at the Hutan Kampung toll plaza on Oct 7.
He said police had intercepted a Proton X70 SUV suspected of carrying five migrants, but the driver allegedly tried to run over a police officer before crashing into the toll barrier.
“Police fired one shot at the tyre. The motorist fled and abandoned the vehicle in Pendang, about 28.3km from the scene,” he said.
Adzli said several people had been detained. Police are looking for two more men to assist in the investigation.
c572fa7c9bbacaef: ALOR SETAR, Oct 12 — An allegation that an 18-year-old youth had stolen a motorcycle is believed to have prompted a group of suspects to torture him before his body was found by the roadside in Jalan Harvard, Gurun, last Thursday.

“The victim was caught in Pendang on October 5 before being taken to the house of one of the suspects, where he was detained for two days, tortured and beaten, and had his hair cut,” he told reporters at the Kedah Contingent Police Headquarters here today.

Police seized 14 mobile phones, a Honda City, scissors and the victim’s identity card. Twelve suspects have been remanded for six days until Wednesday, while two underage suspects have been remanded until tomorrow. The case is being investigated under Section 302 of the Penal Code.

e04a1e278c8b306b: KUCHING: Kerajaan Sarawak akan bekerjasama rapat dengan kerajaan persekutuan untuk memajukan cadangan Zon Ekonomi Khas (SEZ) Sibu, dengan rundingan rasmi dijangka menentukan insentif pelaburan, mekanisme pemudahcaraan serta keperluan infrastruktur strategik bagi zon berkenaan.
Premier Sarawak Abang Johari Openg berkata, kerjasama itu akan membabitkan kementerian dan agensi persekutuan yang berkaitan bagi membangunkan SEZ Sibu sebagai model transformasi ekonomi serantau.

Beliau turut menyambut baik persetujuan kerajaan persekutuan terhadap cadangan Sarawak itu, menyifatkannya sebagai mencerminkan perkongsian erat antara Putrajaya dengan Kuching dalam merealisasikan potensi ekonomi Sarawak tengah.

“Saya juga ingin merakamkan penghargaan kepada perdana menteri dan kerajaan persekutuan kerana bersetuju dengan cadangan Sarawak untuk menubuhkan Zon Ekonomi Khas Sibu,” katanya ketika membentangkan Belanjawan Sarawak 2027 pada sidang DUN hari ini.

Pada Jumaat lepas, Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim ketika membentangkan Belanjawan 2027 mengumumkan bahawa perbincangan rasmi akan dimulakan dengan Sarawak bagi memuktamadkan kerangka insentif pelaburan, menubuhkan pusat pemudahcaraan pelaburan sehenti serta mengenal pasti keperluan infrastruktur strategik bagi zon ekonomi yang dicadangkan itu.

Abang Johari berkata, SEZ Sibu akan meletakkan semula Sibu sebagai hab pertumbuhan ekonomi moden bagi Sarawak tengah, dengan tumpuan kepada sektor pembuatan bernilai tinggi, pemprosesan hiliran, industri berasaskan pertanian, logistik dan ekonomi hijau.

Inisiatif itu, katanya, dijangka menarik pelaburan berkualiti dari dalam dan luar negara, mewujudkan peluang pekerjaan berkemahiran dengan gaji yang baik serta memberi perusahaan kecil dan sederhana (PKS) tempatan akses kepada pasaran dan rantaian bekalan baharu.
f35a8e942dfc3844: VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo XIV will be admitted to hospital on Tuesday morning for an operation to remove a lump from his lung, the Vatican said.
The 71-year-old Leo announced on Sunday after his weekly prayers that he would undergo an operation "in the coming days".
Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni told AFP on Monday that the pontiff would be admitted on "Tuesday, late morning".
The surgery to remove a pulmonary nodule, or small growth of tissue in the lung, will mark the pope's first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025.
It is expected to take place at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, north of the Vatican, which has a dedicated papal suite.
In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told assembled crowds that doctors had discovered the nodule "at a very early stage" during recent medical checks.
"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene, and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it," he said from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace.
The Vatican's press office has said that the pope's recovery time could be about a week.
11deca28ce643037: KOTA KINABALU: Sabah must balance economic development with environmental protection and strengthen climate resilience to ensure sustainable growth, says chief minister Hajiji Noor.
Hajiji said coastal cities, which serve as hubs for trade, tourism and other economic activities, faced growing risks from rising sea levels, extreme weather, and pollution.

“With proper planning and close cooperation, we can develop safer, cleaner and more resilient cities for future generations,” he said in a speech read by assistant minister to the chief minister, Joniston Bangkuai, at the opening of the Kota Kinabalu International Mayor’s Dialogue 2026 here today.
The event brings together participants from eight countries and 15 cities, including representatives from Indonesia, South Korea and the US.
Hajiji said climate change considerations must be integrated into urban management, including drainage, sanitation, flood control, and the conservation of mangroves and rivers.

This would require better access to climate financing, stronger public-private partnerships and greater knowledge-sharing between cities to support green infrastructure projects and improve climate resilience.
He said Sabah’s waters sustain livelihoods, food security, and various maritime industries, making their protection crucial to long-term economic sustainability.
The state is also part of the Coral Triangle, one of the world’s richest marine biodiversity regions.

Hajiji said the state government’s commitment to balancing conservation and economic development was reflected in the Tun Mustapha Park, which protects marine ecosystems while supporting local communities.

The Sabah Blue Economy agenda also offers opportunities for sustainable growth in fisheries, aquaculture, marine biotechnology, coastal and island tourism, and logistics, he said, adding that these activities must be developed responsibly.
He said the agenda aligned with the Sabah Maju Jaya 2.0 development plan for 2026-2030, which focusses on strengthening income sources and improving public welfare.
It also complemented the Sabah Biotechnology Action Plan 2024-2034, which links biodiversity conservation with socio-economic development.
Hajiji also commended Kota Kinabalu City Hall for advancing its Smart City agenda through technologies such as artificial intelligence, digital twins, geospatial tools, and urban data platforms.
He said these technologies could improve early flood warning systems, land-use planning and public service delivery.
“However, digital transformation must remain people-centred, transparent and accountable,” he said.
fdeacd4e30e02065: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — The Finance Ministry will use amendments to the Audit Act 1957 and the Government Procurement Act 2026 to strengthen oversight of public funds and improve transparency in government spending.

Treasury secretary-general Tan Sri Johan Mahmood Merican said the amended Audit Act gives the Auditor-General greater scope to trace funds across government agencies and examine how the money is used.
“The government has also approved the Government Procurement Act, which enables the government to tighten oversight in terms of transparency and value for money in the procurement process.
“The Act will be enforced next year, where the government will also share details on companies receiving the contracts,” Johan said.

The Government Procurement Act 2026 was gazetted on May 26 and is expected to come into operation in 2027, subject to a commencement date appointed by the Finance Minister through a gazette notification.

Johan said governance would be further strengthened through a proposed Government-Owned Entities Bill, which is intended to improve oversight of procurement and investment by government-owned entities, including government-linked companies and statutory bodies.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim had previously said the proposed Bill was intended to prevent major financial scandals, including 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB), and mismanagement involving Tabung Haji and Felda, from recurring.

Separately, Anwar said the Government Procurement Act would improve transparency through the publication of project details, including the names of contractors and contract values, once it comes into force in 2027.
“When governance is corrected, the benefits resulting from the change will contribute to the people’s welfare,” Anwar said previously.
3a228466c214dfd8: London's minicab drivers want Mayor Sadiq Khan to put the brakes on robotaxis before they threaten thousands of jobs, with a new City Hall report casting doubt on whether the capital is ready for driverless cars. The Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB) has called on Transport for London (TfL) to halt the rollout following the publication of a London Assembly Transport Committee report on Monday. The 66-page report makes uncomfortable reading for the companies hoping to unleash fleets of driverless taxis on London's streets. "As it stands, we currently have not heard sufficient evidence to persuade us that London should welcome autonomous passenger services," it concludes. Google's Waymo, British startup Wayve, and Chinese tech giant Baidu are among those gearing up to bring autonomous passenger services to London. Waymo has already been testing its cars in the capital and hopes to launch a commercial fleet of "low hundreds" this year, subject to regulatory approval. Uber and Wayve have secured TfL private hire licenses for vehicles offering supervised self-driving rides, meaning a human driver remains legally in control, and Freenow and Baidu are targeting a fully driverless launch in 2027. London has around 105,000 licensed private hire drivers, many of whom have reason to worry about cars that can do their jobs without them. "Every car feeds a family, and the prospect of not being able to earn money leaves us all with a deep uncertainty as to how we will provide for them. We already struggle to get by as it is," said Gholomreza "Rez" Kamyabi, an Uber driver and vice chair of the IWGB Private Hire Drivers union. The committee heard warnings that robotaxis could put large numbers of drivers out of work, and wants TfL to work with unions and operators to retrain, redeploy, and fund those affected. The IWGB, however, wants the rollout stopped. "The IWGB Private Hire Drivers Union opposes the rollout of driverless cars," said union president Alex Marshall, warning the technology could put thousands out of work while benefiting tech companies and investors. Jobs aren't the only concern. Under the government's interim Automated Passenger Services permitting scheme, the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) issues operating permits. TfL must consent before a service launches in London, but cannot independently suspend or revoke a permit once issued. TfL also has no formal say over existing driverless trials, and operators aren't legally required to report incidents to it, although some have shared information voluntarily. The report details several incidents involving autonomous test vehicles, including a car reportedly entering a police crime scene cordon in April, another filmed turning the wrong way into a one-way street in June, and a reported collision with a motorcycle in July. It also questions how robotaxis would handle medical emergencies, passenger safety, and accessibility. None of the autonomous vehicles currently being trialed are wheelchair accessible. Then there's congestion. Robotaxis could lure passengers away from public transportation while adding more traffic as vehicles travel empty between fares. The committee wants operators to report their empty mileage so TfL can assess the impact. Londoners aren't exactly clamoring for the technology either. A YouGov survey commissioned by the committee found that 42 percent opposed autonomous passenger vehicles, compared with 29 percent who supported them. Just 29 percent said they would be likely to use one. The committee stopped short of calling for a ban, instead recommending tougher safety requirements, giving TfL powers to cap vehicle numbers, and a process to request the immediate suspension of permits. It also wants TfL to take over permitting when the Automated Vehicles Act is fully implemented, expected in the second half of 2027. At the time of the investigation, TfL had not yet published the criteria it would use to approve driverless passenger services. So London is preparing for robotaxis while its transport authority works out the rules, Assembly members question the benefits, and cab drivers demand the whole thing be stopped. Still, at least the cars won't complain about their working conditions.®

1f5cca64f821507b: PARIS, Oct 12 — Some 130 French high schools remained closed today, the education ministry said, with authorities hoping the protest movement that has rocked the nation in recent weeks would ease ahead of half-term holidays.

Students have blocked entrances to hundreds of lycees — high schools for children aged 15 to 18 — in recent weeks, with squads of riot police deployed and occasionally violent clashes resulting.

Piling dumpsters, bins and barriers in front of their schools, or carrying often humorous signs at protests, pupils have complained about absent teachers, overloaded timetables, overcrowded classes and dilapidated classrooms, among other grievances.
Pupils were blocking the entrances of schools in Paris, the southern cities of Marseille and Toulouse and the western city of Rennes, AFP reporters saw.

“We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression,” said 16-year-old pupil Emeline.
Student rallies have been planned for Tuesday, ahead of wider public demonstrations against the rising cost of living that are expected on Saturday.

“These are issues that deserve time, consultation, discussion, and respect,” Macron said.
“This also requires that it be done calmly, in an orderly way, and with respect for both people and property.”
Fewer schools closed
The education ministry said 96.5 percent of France’s 3,700 lycees remained open on Monday.
“The number of school closures is falling,” with 96.5 percent of schools open on Monday, yet “the violence is intensifying”, it said.
The ministry said some eight members of teaching staff had been injured on Monday morning, mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, it said.
These incidents did not include the shooting in Aubagne, which police said did not appear to be linked to the student protest movement.
Most of the demonstrations in recent weeks have been peaceful, but some protesters have started fires and vandalised bus shelters.
In response, police have used tear gas, batons and blast balls, leading to accusations from rights groups and students of a disproportionate use of force.
The government last week promised some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
A government spokeswoman on Monday said they had started to be assigned.
The police have opened internal investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators since the protest movement began last month.
More than 6,800 people — largely minors — have been taken into police custody, the justice ministry says. — AFP

4716b75a3ed74c46: A piece of internet history that once traveled strapped to a pigeon's leg is up for auction at Christie's, where someone has already bid $4,000 for what might be the world's most expensive ping. The unusual lot is a surviving IP packet from a 2001 experiment in which Norwegian Linux enthusiasts decided to find out whether the internet could, in fact, run on birds. The idea dates back to April 1, 1990, when American network engineer David Waitzman published RFC 1149, titled A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams on Avian Carriers. Written in the wonderfully dry language of an official internet standards document, the April Fools' proposal outlined how carrier pigeons could transport IP datagrams between locations. It noted that avian carriers could provide high bandwidth, although latency would be another matter entirely. Most people appreciated the joke and moved on. The Bergen Linux User Group (BLUG), however, decided to actually build the thing. On April 28, 2001, the group put RFC 1149 to the test using racing pigeons, printers, and scanners. IP packets were printed as hexadecimal strings on strips of paper, attached to the birds' legs, and flown between two lofts 5km (roughly 3 miles) apart. The results hardly amounted to a ringing endorsement of pigeon-powered networking. Nine packets were dispatched, but only four replies came back, giving the experiment a packet-loss rate of about 56 percent. Still, the network worked, at least in the loosest possible sense of the word. Actual IP packets had traveled through the air without a single router, fiber-optic cable, or telecoms provider getting involved. One of those packets has now resurfaced at auction house Christie's as part of its Fine Printed Books & Manuscripts Including Americana and Science auction. The item is a small scroll of paper measuring just 41mm by 210mm, complete with creases from being rolled up and attached to the pigeon's leg. It is now framed, with an inscription on the reverse identifying it as the property of Waitzman, to whom it was presented in 2002. Christie's initially estimated the packet would fetch between $2,000 and $3,000, but bidding has already reached $4,000. The auction closes on October 13. The auction house describes the experiment as an example of the internet's tradition of the "artful hack," celebrating the technical ingenuity and sense of humor of its early community. There is, of course, something rather fitting about an internet packet that took to the skies 25 years ago now commanding thousands of dollars. Most packets disappear into the ether once they've served their purpose. This one ended up in a frame and is being sold by Christie's. Not bad for something delivered by a pigeon. ®

b775ce65b1401b58: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 12 — The government aims to improve the Water Quality Index (WQI) of 33 rivers identified as polluted in 2025 by at least 10 per cent within a year, with appropriate recognition to be given to state governments that achieve the target.

Anwar said discussions also covered expanding trade and investment, including a potential free trade agreement (FTA), tariff restructuring, stronger supply chains and cooperation in energy, transport, the halal industry and tourism.
Anwar said he and King Abdullah also exchanged views on geopolitical developments in West Asia, particularly in Palestine and Syria, and their implications for regional security and stability.
He said they also agreed on the urgent need to end atrocities against Palestinians, including continued violence and rights violations in Jerusalem and the West Bank.
“I stressed that Malaysia will remain steadfast in championing Palestinian rights while strengthening humanitarian assistance, particularly for the people of Gaza,” he said.
Anwar noted that the Jordanian monarch also expressed appreciation for Malaysia’s stance and efforts in supporting the Palestinian cause.

Anwar also expressed hope that the meeting would elevate Malaysia-Jordan relations through closer economic and technological cooperation, as well as shared commitments to humanity, peace and global justice.
The state visit was King Abdullah’s second to Malaysia since May 2008, as both countries marked more than six decades of diplomatic relations established in 1965.

Prior to his departure after concluding the visit, King Abdullah granted Anwar an audience at the Bunga Raya Complex, Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA), for about 30 minutes to discuss strengthening longstanding bilateral relations.
Bilateral trade reached RM993.4 million in 2025, up 15.2 per cent from 2024, while trade from January to August 2026 rose eight per cent year-on-year to RM740.7 million. — Bernama

71f94acff13d7968: GUA MUSANG, Oct 12 — Old birth certificates, including handwritten documents issued in paper format, remain valid and do not need to be replaced, said National Registration Department (NRD) director-general Datuk Badrul Hisham Alias.

27609d0c902b962c: ALOR SETAR, Oct 12 — Kedah police successfully crippled an online scam syndicate involving suspects posing as Indian police officers during a raid on a business premises in Bandar Putra, Kulim, last Friday.

Kedah Police Chief Datuk Adzli Abu Shah said that during the joint operation at 8pm, police arrested 48 individuals suspected of acting as syndicate members, comprising seven locals, eight Indian nationals, and 33 Pakistani nationals.
“This syndicate began operating late last August at a three-story shoplot running online scam activities by impersonating as police officers from India, targeting victims from that country.

“They used the Telegram app to communicate and deceive victims by claiming the victims’ phone numbers were involved in illegal activities. Victims were asked to transfer money into provided bank accounts for police investigation purposes,” he told reporters at the Kedah Contingent Police Headquarters (IPK) here today.

He added that investigations into the syndicate members, aged 20 to 43, revealed that they claimed they were duped after applying for jobs offered on social media before being added to a Telegram group and promised salaries of around RM2,500 to RM3,500 a month.

“Investigations also found that the syndicate members failed to present valid travel documents for entry into Malaysia. So far, a total of 73 individuals have fallen victim to this syndicate’s scams, involving losses of nearly RM1.4 million.

“Additionally, police seized various items including 89 mobile phones, seven laptops, modems, monitors, Indian police uniforms, Indian flags, Indian Central Bureau of Investigation flags, and several other items. The total value of the seizures is estimated at RM70,000,” he said.

4f02e73424376278: STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 — American economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize today for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” the jury at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said in a statement.

“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, chair of the prize committee, said in the statement.

During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models long used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations no longer worked.
That prompted Hall and Woodford to develop new tools for understanding which policy responses could be the most effective.

“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy jury said.
“This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.”
The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.
It was created instead through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968, leading detractors to dub it “a false Nobel”.
But like the Nobels in chemistry and physics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winner and follows the same selection process.
Last year, the award went to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France’s Philippe Aghion and Canada’s Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth.
Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million cheque.
The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will. — AFP
3e0ea74af87cd491: BERLIN, Oct 12 — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government faced new turbulence on Monday when a key minister from its junior coalition partner, the SPD, unexpectedly quit and criticised “attacks” from the chancellor’s party.
Baerbel Bas, labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left SPD, cited personal reasons for her resignation, saying she needed time to grieve following the death of her daughter-in-law.
But she also took aim at Merz’s conservative CDU.

“I must unfortunately note that the public attacks against me — regrettably including those from within the ranks of our coalition partner — have continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally,” she said.
The resignation comes amid turmoil for the government, which is grappling with a sluggish economy and low poll ratings.
The far-right AfD has also soundly beaten the CDU in two recent state polls, including in the region of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania where Merz’s party scored its worst ever result.
CDU politicians have accused Bas of holding up planned changes to working time regulations and pension reform.
“You can only expect criticism in that case,” the CDU leader of Rhineland-Palatinate state, Gordon Schnieder, told Welt TV on Monday, after Bas quit.
The departure risks complicating pension reform, one of the coalition’s main priorities.
Bas’s ministry is preparing a draft bill after a government commission recommended people work longer to cope with the fact that the population is aging.
Bas is giving up her posts as both a minister and co-leader of the SPD.
She will be replaced as labour minister by Alexander Schweitzer, one of the SPD’s vice chairs, party sources told AFP.
She intends to retain her seat as an MP for Duisburg, a city at the heart of the former Ruhr mining region in northern Germany.
Merz said on X he respected Bas’s decision, adding: “I thank her for her commitment.
“As a father and a grandfather, I can only imagine how heavily this loss weighs. I wish her and her family a lot of strength.” — AFP
4022cac2a44fa81a: COPENHAGEN, Oct 12 — Greenland’s foreign minister said today that US claims to the territory had ruptured “trust” with the superpower that needed rebuilding.

Restoring trust “will be a difficult undertaking”, he added.

He said the United States would build two “major” bases on the autonomous Arctic territory of 57,000 people.
“A certain momentum emerged after the summer holidays and the end of summer, which made it possible to reach an agreement,” Egede said.

The Greenlandic parliament was scheduled to start its debate on the accord on Monday but the Danish parliament has not yet put it on the its agenda. — AFP

a3f54fe845f85096: As the world’s billionaires anxiously plot datacenters to run trillions of lines of AI-generated slop code, one software engineer has zagged in a completely different direction: building an ecosystem for writing and running small apps that run on desktop computers, like it was 1992 all over again. Self-described “maker of things” Tarwin Stroh-Spijer has created a JavaScript runtime, called TinyJS, for making very small applications (many occupying ~6MB or less on disk) for macOS, Linux or Windows. To be clear, TinyJS is not a “no code” framework with hobbled capabilities. It offers the full programming power of JavaScript, along with the visual rendering and communication capabilities of the underlying OS. The trick to TinyJS’s frugality is that it uses the WebView window of each OS, utilizing the built-in browser engine to visually render the app, rather than implementing a UI layer from scratch. It uses WebKit to run apps in this fashion on macOS, WebView2 for Windows, and WebKitGTK for Linux. TinyJS’s approach is starkly different from using the Electron framework, which bundles a Chromium open source browser core with each desktop app. But whereas Electron promises an identical look-and-feel of an app across all platforms, TinyJS apps will have slight visual variances when run on the different platforms, owing to minor differences in how each OS’s rendering engine works. The Electron app pays for this cross-platform uniformity: with Electron, even the most basic application can weigh 150MB. Rust is not always the answer The core of TinyJS is txiki.js, an ultra-compact JavaScript runtime written by Saúl Ibarra Corretgé that makes Deno and Bun look like behemoths. The starter package is about 5.6MB and the launcher takes up another megabyte or so. The rest of the package is all developer code, basically. Stroh-Spijer also simplified the development process by using the OS’ interprocess communication mechanisms for handling data transfer, eliminating the need to bundle an HTTP server for each app, along with all the security headaches that entails. All coding in TinyJS is done in JavaScript, CSS and HTML – no compiling necessary. There’s plenty of room for creativity here, as web design capabilities have been growing by leaps and bounds of late. The Tauri project has a similar aim of creating the tiny apps, and can deliver a desktop app in 10MB, but that framework has some drawbacks, Stroh-Spijer noted on the TinyJS website. The main one is that you have to write applications in Rust – which requires learning Rust, among other drawbacks. Also, TinyJS hands over a lot of the app’s substrate to the OS – such as dialogs, menus, tray, clipboard, auto-updates – that with Tauri would have to be imported one plugin at a time. Developers don’t need Node.js as a dependency here, unless they want to run a framework that requires it, such as Vite. It can also support other JavaScript frameworks like React, Vue, and Svelte. Or it can run with no dependencies at all. You can also use TinyJS to wrap a Webpage, by pointing the window to a URL. Imagine having your favourite site as an app on your desktop. A shelf of diminutive apps With TinyJS, Stroh-Spijer created an “app store” that can be run, natch, from the desktop (the zipped Windows version can be downloaded here). As of press time, it indexes 25 sample apps he wrote. The example apps, all free, vary in utility and whimsy. The shelf includes a world clock (which ships as a 3.8MB zip file), a clipboard history app (3.7MB), a markdown editor (4.9MB), a desktop ghost (3.8MB), a SQLite browser (4.1MB) and, most impressively, a clone of the iconic Winamp music player, which demands only 7.4MB from your hard drive. Once you convince Windows Defender to trust the launcher, you can download and open the app of your choice directly from the shelf. In my tests, the copy-and-paste app, clearly written for Mac hotkeys, was still too buggy for Windows, though the world clock ran just fine and consumed only 15.5MB of RAM on my box. (Caveat emptor: the launcher checks the hash to ensure the validity of downloaded apps, though you’re trusting that Stroh-Spijer harbors no evil intent here). Or, just skip the examples and build your own test apps. Today’s personal computers are powerful, but there are still many good reasons for building apps that would be petite even by last century's standards. Commercial applications (those still around anyway) and Web browsers are voracious RAM consumers, so adding more tools to the desktop with little overhead is a positive. Plus, unlike the bloaty apps, minuscule apps start fast, and, in theory, draw less power on laptops. And just like the TikTok meme of the woman who insists on bringing her dog on the plane because it’s just “a tiny dog,” users may want to add these apps to their desktops, because, well, they’re tiny. ®
b88b21b5c829ef7a: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars.

The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements. If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones, robotic landers, communication satellites, and a nuclear power plant; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water.

Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.”

The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved?

But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher.
SELMAN DESIGN

But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.

Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed?

The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.

Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.

But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?”

Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions.
The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe.
Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night.

Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms.

The first is galactic cosmic rays, which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation.

Then you have the sun. It may sustain life on Earth, but without our planet’s thick atmosphere and magnetic bubble to get in its way, moonwalkers will occasionally be blasted by one of its paroxysms: a solar flare (a burst of diverse types of radiation) or a coronal mass ejection (volleys of magnetized plasma). “During Apollo, they knew that if a large solar flare occurred while the crew was on the moon, there would be no way to keep them alive,” says Metzger. The crew could have developed acute radiation sickness and perished in a matter of days.

The way to survive a powerful solar flare or coronal mass ejection is straightforward: “Get back inside a habitat where there’s more shielding,” says George—preferably a dedicated, highly shielded “storm shelter,” essentially a thick-walled bunker. The issue is that astronauts might be outside the base, driving a rover many miles away. Coronal mass ejections take hours to days to reach the vicinity of the Earth-moon system, but solar flares can do so in under an hour. And scientists can’t yet model the sun well enough to give much advance notice. “All of the capability to forecast solar storms is kind of like where weather forecasting [was] … in the ’50s and ’60s,” says George.

As for those punchy galactic cosmic rays, the only way to avoid them would be to put a lot of stuff—lunar rocks, possibly—between the astronauts and the sky. “Build habitat modules underground,” says Chris Dreyer, director of engineering at the Center for Space Resources at the Colorado School of Mines. One option: Burrow living quarters into lava tubes, the naturally hollowed-­out volcanic tunnels created by molten rock eons ago. At this point, NASA hasn’t mentioned any plans to make its moon base subterranean, but it may need to if it wants to end up with a small lunar city.

Radiation limits the time astronauts can spend on the lunar surface over their entire life—it can total around two years max, experts estimate, before the health risk becomes too high. Unfortunately, that’s not all space will throw at them. When the Artemis II astronauts swung around the far side of the moon earlier this year, they saw curious flashes light up the silvery land below. These were the explosive deaths of small meteoroids punching into the lunar surface.

Earth is naturally protected from smaller space rocks, up to around 50 feet in diameter: They burn up inconsequentially in the atmosphere. “You don’t have that option on the moon,” says Philip Lubin, a physicist and planetary defense researcher at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Since smaller rocks plunge toward planets and moons far more frequently than larger ones do, this means the moon is often peppered by what are effectively tiny space bullets. They could easily puncture a spacesuit or the engine of a moon rover.

How do you protect astronauts from the onslaught? “The simplest answer is burial,” says Nicholas Schmerr, a planetary seismologist at the University of Maryland—conveniently, the same way you’d deal with radiation exposure. Pile up moon rocks onto your base walls or put habitable structures in lava tubes.

Inconveniently, there’s always a chance that a bigger asteroid will come along. Even buried habitation modules would have trouble surviving an assault from a 50-footer—about the length of a semi-trailer.

That doesn’t mean a moon base would be helpless against bigger asteroids. Planetary defense has come a long way in just a few decades. NASA’s DART mission demonstrated that it could deflect an asteroid by ramming into the rock with an uncrewed spacecraft, and cutting-­edge experiments at clandestine labs around the US suggest that a nuclear bomb could swat away or entirely vaporize errant space rocks. An array of both ground-based and space-based telescopes specifically designed to spy killers—such as the ATLAS quartet of largely automated telescopes, and the soon-to-be-launched NEO Surveyor infrared telescope—are also aiming to find 90% of the near-Earth asteroids potentially capable of wiping out entire cities (those 460 feet across) in the coming years.

All these protections apply to the moon. But asteroids 50 feet across are so stealthy that even NASA’s best telescopes would struggle to see them years or even months in advance. Odds are that they would first be seen not long before they were due to hit the lunar surface. Then what?

It’s not unreasonable to imagine several turret-like launch sites on the moon that, owing to the lower gravity and airless environment, could rapidly fire projectiles toward an incoming asteroid. Hit it hard enough and it would break into fragments. Just make sure you shoot when it is as far away as possible: “If you were to break something up into a thousand pieces, then you have a thousand impacts on the moon,” says Lubin. “That might be worse than letting it hit one place.”
Having your base destroyed by an asteroid would be awful. But a moon base is far more likely to be imperiled by dust—which, unlike asteroids, is everywhere, all the time.

Volcanic lunar rocks, when broken down, turn into sharp, electrostatically charged, adhesive, acrid, abrasive particles. While on the moon, Apollo astronauts who inhaled some of this dust occasionally suffered from a strange “lunar hay fever,” which irritated their eyes and agitated their lungs. That same dust ate through all kinds of gear with disturbing ease. “It rips up seals, gears, motors, spacesuits, habitats—everything else it comes into contact with,” says Justin Cyrus, the CEO of Lunar Outpost, a spaceflight technology company that is providing NASA with one of the Artemis program’s moon rovers.

NASA has already developed a defense against these dark shards: the electrodynamic dust shield, or EDS. The lightweight electrodes that make up this shield—which can be layered on machinery, walls, and perhaps even spacesuits—use opposing currents to blast away the electrically charged dust. The EDS worked wonders when tested in labs on Earth, and it also demonstrated its anti-dust magic when sent to the lunar surface in 2025 as part of a NASA-sponsored robotic mission.

Amy Fritz, a dust-mitigation researcher at Johnson Space Center, says that the EDS will likely be widely featured all over a lunar habitat. But other dust-fighting instruments are being developed too—including a lint-roller-type object inspired by gecko skin and a sci-fi-esque blaster that uses ionized nitrogen gas. Its first spray will neutralize the charge of the dust to remove its stickiness; then a second burst will clear it off the surface.

Irritatingly, the busier a base gets, the dustier things will become. As it expands to the size of a small city, rocket ships will need to deliver cargo and crew to the lunar surface on a frequent cadence. Each takeoff and landing will launch a salvo of dust in every direction, inundating the base’s infrastructure. “You have to worry about essentially being sandblasted every time,” says Fritz.

Metzger calculates that even with landing pads more than 3,000 feet away from a base, just 10 to 20 liftoffs or landings would be sufficient to severely damage things like protective coatings on exterior walls and communications equipment. After a while, he says, “everything breaks.”

Even if the moon base of the future is buried partly below ground, barricaded against micrometeorites and space radiation, and well equipped with dust-repelling technologies, it’s still a risky gig for any astronaut. Skipping around in a preternaturally agile way at one-sixth of Earth’s gravity will be entertaining. But “microgravity is not good for the human body,” says Dreyer. Muscle wastage, cardiovascular troubles, respiratory problems, and immune deficiencies can arise.

Radiation, too, may always afflict lunar residents. And there’s also evidence that disease-causing microbes could stealthily sneak aboard spacecraft, even after stringent sterilization procedures. Those microbes may behave differently than they do on Earth; microgravity experiments (both real and simulated) have suggested that some become more aggressive and more likely to cause disease. “We call them the invisible crew,” says Lisa Carnell, the director of NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division.
NASA/GSFC/MIT

Hoping to find a better way to protect astronauts, Carnell spearheaded an experiment called AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response), which launched aboard the Artemis II mission. It used thumb-drive-size chips, containing cells taken from the heart, lungs, or other parts of the body, that could be switched on to act like miniature organs. Scientists have previously used this organ-on-a-chip technology for purposes like testing out new pharmaceuticals in a highly controlled setting. For Artemis II, Carnell’s crew sent up chips containing bone marrow samples taken from the mission’s four astronauts. Bone marrow makes red and white blood cells, as well as platelets—the sort of stuff that affects almost the entire human body. So seeing how space radiation and microgravity affect it would give Carnell and her team vital insight into how astronauts’ biology might change on the moon.

The advantage of organ chips is that you can make them for any astronaut and then send them into space ahead of time to see how that person’s organs will react to spaceflight. Researchers envision that data from such chips will be able to clue medics in to the specific preventive treatments or pharmaceuticals that will help moonbound astronauts on their journey.

What is NASA likely to send up sooner rather than later? “Brain organoids,” says Carnell. Yes, she adds—that sounds super weird. But it would be good to know how a real brain might respond to being on the moon for several months before people start living there.

Okay. Your vast moon base and its inhabitants are protected—as much as is possible—from the treacherous lunar environment. But astronauts’ time is extremely valuable, and humans are fragile creatures. You can’t make them do all the heavy lifting, which means that whether you’re trying to make a tiny lunar outpost or a small city, you’re going to need a lot of robots. “The buildup of the moon base, in the first years, will pretty much 99% be robotic,” says NASA’s García-Galán.

Autonomy will be there right from the start. NASA’s new version of the moon buggy, its Lunar Terrain Vehicle, can be driven by the astronauts riding in it but can also be piloted remotely from Earth (or from elsewhere on the moon). There are visions, too, of adding modular robotic arms, towing vehicles, and cargo movers—all still in the preliminary stages of planning.

Over the next few decades, though, we’ll likely want an army of robots to do our bidding: excavators to dig up lunar rocks that could be turned into concrete and bricks, plus other robots to flatten surfaces, dig trenches, create building foundations, pave landing pads, and build up dust-deflecting berms to keep the base from being sandblasted by launches and landings. Even solar panels and wiring can potentially be made from moon rocks—something that the spaceflight company Blue Origin demonstrated in labs on Earth in 2023 using a geologic simulant designed to match the composition of lunar regolith.

Powering this robot army will require considerable energy. Two-week-long nights make solar power an impractical solution. Aside from a cornucopia of high-­capacity, extreme-temperature-resistant batteries, nuclear power is probably the only viable option. A small, car-size nuclear reactor, filled with an almost literal handful of uranium, could power a small village for a decade without needing to be refueled. And although nobody’s yet tested a nuclear reactor on the moon, few doubt that NASA and the US Department of Energy can conjure up a working design—one that perhaps wouldn’t be too different from those aboard nuclear submarines. A moon base in 2100 would probably feature multiple small, autonomously or remotely operated nuclear reactors, which—conveniently—the base-expanding robots could simply plug themselves into to recharge.

But the biggest lunar question mark might be water, which planners want to support the astronauts—and to make fuel to launch things from the lunar surface. A process known as electrolysis, which uses electricity to snap apart molecular bonds, can be used to split water into oxygen and hydrogen, both of which could be used to make rocket fuel. Getting them this way could be far less expensive than sending either all the way from Earth. And as an added bonus, it would provide a source of breathable oxygen.

Orbital data has revealed that there is some amount of water preserved in patches on the lunar south pole, but little is known about how much there actually is, what form it takes, or how easy it will be to extract. Will there be solid sheets of ice here and there, ready for us to excavate? Or will there be scattered ice crystals intermingled among the rocky grains, requiring some more inventive form of extraction?
a9a81b0b54c0074b: It's 1988. Windows 2.0 is a DOS shell that runs on a dual-floppy 8086 PC. VGA is the aspirational video standard. A three-man startup in East London has decided to create low-cost LANs. There's not much of that and not much by way of standards, which is why a young programmer is rather excited by an emerging contender called TCP/IP. He's particularly keen because he's just finished implementing IBM's PC networking API, NetBIOS, which hurt almost as much as integrating any sort of networking with DOS. Research means library books, magazine articles, and asking questions on Usenet over kilobit dial-up. Getting the wrong idea is easy. Trying to build the TCP/IP stack on the ISO/OSI seven-layer model produces more pain, but sanity prevails, and after a bit, there's a working network. Nearly 40 years later, the once-young programmer is now a curmudgeonly Reg columnist. Floppies have become terabyte thumb drives. Kilobit modems are gigabit fiber and Wi-Fi. Graphics have come on a bit too. And he hasn't touched Windows or an Intel CPU in years. It is a transformed world. Except for one thing – everything talks to everything over TCP/IP. It's time to celebrate the digital oxygen of the global data ecosystem. TCP/IP is still newsworthy. Any apparent attempt to replace part of it is worth reporting, in this case a congestion-easing protocol called Homa superseding TCP. Only it's not a replacement, just an alternative designed to run alongside. That this is possible is due to one of the genius decisions made as TCP/IP evolved – splitting what was one protocol into two: TCP and IP. IP, the Internet Protocol, just sends packets between two addresses, best effort, no guarantees when, in what order, or even if they'll get through. The Transmission Control Protocol uses IP but delivers a reliable, ordered stream of bytes, arranging retransmission of missing data. Thus, if you don't like how TCP does things, you can add your own IP-speaking protocol to run alongside. This approach also saw TCP/IP vanquish rival protocols from very large industry incumbents, such as IBM's Systems Network Architecture (SNA) and ATM – Asynchronous Transfer Mode – from the telecoms side. Packet-switched IP can't possibly succeed, they said, with its non-deterministic transmissions of unknown latency. Nothing reliable could be built on that. TCP/IP, being open, flexible, and built by consensus by individual, inspired engineers, just got on with being useful. That had been proved on January 1, 1983, when ARPANET – the proto internet – dropped the proto when it switched over wholesale from its own NCP to TCP/IP. Known as flag days, such events weren't uncommon as previously isolated early networks had to adapt or die to the new interconnected world. TCP/IP was explicitly designed to inter-network, from the seminal paper [PDF] in 1974 by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn. From that 13-page paper to adoption across ARPANET took nine years. Five years later, a greenhorn coder could build the stack for completely novel hardware in three months. It took longer to work out how to build an installable driver for IBM's PS/2 Micro Channel Architecture. The future wasn't hard to see. Once it had beaten the opposition, the extremely practical, extremely open soul of TCP/IP repeatedly saved it from its biggest enemy. Itself. It turned out that once we had a technology that could freely connect any number of devices to each other, end to end, we wanted to do that very much. The internet, freed of central control and gatekeepers, grew exponentially, especially after another protocol, HTTP, shyly perched on top of TCP. Naysayers predicted letting ordinary people use this would clog the internet, to the point that the introduction of image tags was seen as portending the End Times. Congestion collapse could close it all down. Fortunately, shortly before Tim Berners-Lee began work on the Web, a 1988 paper by Van Jacobson and Mike Karels, Congestion Avoidance and Control [PDF], came up with a set of strategies and tweaks to TCP that has kept the problem at bay ever since. A global network with no central control that can fix show-stopping, scale-related problems on the fly is a true wonder. Similarly, IPv4's 32-bit address field with 4.3 billion addresses seemed an over-provision, until suddenly it was nowhere near enough. A new version of IP, IPv6, was introduced in 1995 with addresses as plentiful as grains of sand in the Sahara. The trouble was that if you've got billions of devices, you can't do a flag day. IPv6 proved great for infrastructure, but not the edge. Fortunately, a router kludge called Network Address Translation (NAT) appeared, again at roughly the same time. It broke the end-to-end principle only a little bit, but let the old version of IP, IPv4, run untouched. Let's be frank. It's fugly. But it let many devices share a single public IP address, which is why everything that comes out of the box for normies still rocks IPv4 like it's 1981. Just don't ask what happened to IPv5. There are thousands of ways TCP/IP has evolved, many tiny and a few deeply silly, like RFC 1149 (IP over Avian Carriers), material relating to which is, at the time of writing, up for auction at Christie's. At heart, it is one of mankind's most brilliant technical achievements, the underpinning of everything the connected world can do, built from intelligence, vision, openness, iteration, freedom of thought, freedom of action, a rough consensus and running code. It deserves its own universal day of celebration. Let's make it January 1. Let's call it Flag Day. ®

Whenever I’m away from home I look forward to being reunited with these things: the quirky vase that sits in the window of my study, and the owl candlestick, a birthday gift from my potter friend.
